issues.item: Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me
issues.explanation: For a life-threatening accident in a combat pilot, the threat profile should more plausibly center on accident recurrence, mechanical failure, bodily vulnerability, or generalized hypervigilance. 'Watching others closely for signs that they might harm me' implies an interpersonal assault/paranoia-like threat that is not supported by the trauma type or by the other selected items.

issues.item: Dehumanization: I feel like an object, not like a person
issues.explanation: The negative appraisal set otherwise reflects post-traumatic identity disruption and emotional numbing ('Lost Emotions', 'Identity Loss'). 'I feel like an object, not like a person' is comparatively more characteristic of interpersonal violation or severe dissociation/depersonalization. In this profile it sits awkwardly with the accident trauma and with the other appraisal items, reducing thematic coherence of the node.

vignette: Tama Wiremu was forty-eight when the left engine of his fighter detonated over the Pacific, turning a routine patrol into a violent descent. Smoke filled the canopy, the horizon rolled unpredictably, and forty-seven seconds of crushing gravity preceded his ejection into open water. He survived, but the man who climbed into the cockpit felt irrevocably altered. In the months that followed, Tama noticed a hollowing inside his chest. The sharp focus that once defined his flights vanished, replaced by a flat exhaustion. He tried to shake it off, but the numbness deepened until he began to wonder if he had permanently changed for the worse, permanently scarred in a way that would erase his capacity to feel normal emotions again. He would sit on the edge of his bed, staring at his flight suit, certain that the pilot who used to laugh with his squadron mates was gone, leaving a stranger behind in his own skin. This quiet conviction did not stay confined to his memories. Instead, it bled directly into how his nervous system processed every ordinary moment. His conviction that he was permanently damaged and emotionally hollowed out did not stay confined to his memories; it directly dictated his physiological responses, causing his internal belief of irreversible harm to manifest as relentless external threat monitoring. He began scanning his surroundings with desperate precision, convinced that another catastrophe was always one malfunction away. Over the next two years, those internal shifts hardened into daily habits. At their suburban home in Hawaii, he could no longer relax on the sofa. His eyes constantly tracked the perimeter of every room, noting the location of every door and window. He would leave his car in the driveway with the keys in the ignition, needing a clear, unobstructed path to the street the moment something felt wrong. Even inside his own house, he felt on guard, his shoulders tense while his wife cooked dinner. The cockpit environment offered little relief. During ground school, his mind latched onto the smallest irregularity in the briefing packets as proof that disaster was imminent. His former squadron mates noticed the change. Tama had become rigid, flinching at sudden door slams. What had once been a career of calculated risk was now a daily exercise in survival. The emotional numbness and the conviction that he was fundamentally altered did not just isolate him; they actively sustained his constant state of alarm. Because he believed he would never feel normal again, he treated every silence as a threat waiting to surface, and his hypervigilance became a self-fulfilling prophecy. Now at fifty-four, Tama’s world has narrowed to an exhausting routine of scanning and bracing. He still flies, but the joy of the canopy has been replaced by a meticulous, paranoid calculus. Before he even touches the throttle, he maps three alternate routes out of the cockpit, his fingers tracing the ejection handle and the overhead emergency panel as if they were lifelines. His wife has stopped asking him to watch movies in the theater, noting how he sits rigidly in the back row, eyes fixed on the exit doors. The cycle tightens with every passing month. His conviction that he is permanently damaged means he cannot trust his own calm, so he deliberately heightens his watchfulness, treating his baseline nervous system as an enemy to be overridden. This relentless threat monitoring drains him, leaving him feeling even more disconnected from his former self. He has come to believe that the crash is never over, that his mind and the sky are still falling. What finally brought Tama to my office last Tuesday was a quiet breaking point. He stood in the doorway of his training simulation, hands trembling around the yoke, unable to complete a simple approach because his mind was entirely consumed by mapping emergency egress routes while ignoring the instruments. He had missed his wife’s birthday dinner for the third time in a row, leaving a text that simply read, I have to check the perimeter. He did not want to be this way. He sat in my clinic chair, shoulders tight, eyes already tracking the windows, waiting to see if the room held a safe way out. He is not seeking a cure for a memory, he told me, his voice barely above a whisper. He is asking for a way to stop bracing for a fall that never ends.
